newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-ALPHAND INTRUDES ON AUSTRIAN DOMINATION.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-ALPHAND INTRUDES ON AUSTRIAN DOMINATION.

text.p: Frenchman Luc Alphand prevented total Austrian domination of the first downhill practice at the Alpine skiing world championships on Tuesday when he clocked the second-fastest time.
Austrians filled six of the top seven places with Fritz Strobl quickest in one minute 53.88 seconds on the 3.2 km long Kandahar Banchetta piste.
Werner Franz, Hannes Trinkl, Andreas Schifferer, defending downhill champion Patrick Ortlieb and Josef Strobl all trailed Alphand's time of 1:53.99.

But while the two unrelated Strobls, Franz and Ortlieb already have a starting bib for Saturday's downhill, the final Austrian place will be fought out between Trinkl, Schifferer and super-G bronze medalist Guenther Mader -- who was 12th fastest.
Austria can have five racers in the downhill because the champion qualifies automatically.
"Every time I get to the finish area, a Strobl seems to be in the lead," said Franz, who finished second behind Fritz Strobl twice in Val D'Isere and Kitzbuehel.
"I hope people don't get too excited about us Austrians doing so well in the training. The Italians and the Norwegians also know how to ski well."
Only three nations had skiers in the top 10 -- Austria, France and Italy.
Not all top skiers were happy with the piste after the first of three training runs in sunny and mild temperatures.
Fritz Strobl, winner of two downhills this season and a strong favorite for the title here, said: "This is a great slope, there are a lot of bumps and jumps.
"I didn't ski flat out so I'm really surprised I was so fast. But this gives me confidence. I will definitely improve my jumps on this slope if nothing else."
Alphand, the 1996 downhill bronze medallist from Sierra Nevada, was not impressed. "The middle section is so flat you can't get any speed. It's boring and more of a super-G.
Alphand, nursing a cold and taking antibiotics, said: "I'm not really sick, I just have no power."
Local favorite Kristian Ghedina, winner of three downhills this winter, posted the ninth fastest run. "The piste was so-so and I was also just so-so," he said.
It was not a good outing for Swiss downhillers, with 1993 world champion Urs Lehmann the fastest in 17th place, one ahead of William Besse.
The Swiss have not won a world title since Lehmann's gold in the Morioka championships.

"I don't understand why the course was set like a super-G. I was expecting it to be more exciting," said Besse. He accused the International Ski Federation of fearing crashes and playing it safe with a boring piste.
